newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Poor education limits Australian farm - report.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Poor education limits Australian farm - report.

text.p: Australian farmers' poor education was cutting productivity and inhibiting further training, a report by the nation's top farming body released on Tuesday has found.
"(This limits) our capacity to be flexible, adaptable, and responsive to change," said the National Farmers' Federation report.
Australian farms with qualified managers had an average gross operating surplus of A$85,024 in 1993/94, compared to A$58,768 for other farm businesses, it said.
Farms with managers involved in at least one training programme in a year had a higher gross operating surplus (A$68,102) than those which did not (A$39,788).
The report found Australian farmers were less educated than their overseas rivals and other Australian industries.
It said farms most likely to make changes designed to improve profitability were larger, more profitable with some debt, had more educated managers and more than one person on the management team.
"Farm businesses in the sheep industry are less likely to make a change to practice than those in other sectors," the report said.
"The low prices experienced by the sheep industry and consequent lack of financial resources may partly explain the low percentage of 'changers'."
It said agricultural qualifications were particularly important for new farmers and younger farmers, who could expect to make many changes to their farming practice over their working lifetimes.
The report was released for discussion at the federation's two-day conference in Canberra which began on Tuesday.
